newsitem.title: CANADA: Opposition parties scoff at Canadian budget.
newsitem.headline: Opposition parties scoff at Canadian budget.

text.p: Canadian opposition leaders dismissed the federal budget announced on Tuesday as a disappointment and a sham.

The official opposition, the separatist Bloc Quebecois, said Finance Minister Paul Martin's budget had only a few skimpy measures, doing little for economic development or the poor while dumping spending cuts onto the provinces.
"Paul Martin has chosen to do nothing," Bloc leader Michel Gauthier told reporters as Martin spoke in the House of Commons, Parliament's elected chamber. "It's the provinces who are going to pay."
The third largest party in the House, the populist Reform Party, said it would have cut the deficit faster and gotten on to reducing taxes.
"I call it the fudge-it budget," Reform leader Preston Manning said.

"If this is such a good budget, why don't I see any of the benefits? Where are the jobs this was supposed to produce? Where's the pension benefits when I need them and where's the tax relief? None of those things are delivered in this budget."
Ontario Conservative Finance Minister Ernie Eves criticized Martin's failure to deliver substantial tax cuts.

"We would think there was room for them to reduce taxes of several kinds if they had wanted to. They chose not to," he said in Toronto, mentioning for example personal income taxes and the surplus in the unemployment insurance fund.

The once-ruling federal Conservative Party, reduced to two seats in the House but regaining popularity in the polls, said it was deception to cut spending on one hand and trumpet smaller increases on the other hand.
"It's manipulative. It's a shell game. It's as close to lying as you can get," federal Conservative leader Jean Charest said in Ottawa.
He said he anticipated the federal election campaign, expected this year, would be based on the government's financial record.
The leader of the leftist New Democratic Party, Alexa McDonough, said the government should move beyond the battle of the deficit.
